narrative:
Based on the model’s assessment, your predicted chance of failing the bar exam on the first attempt is 60 percent. In practical terms, the university saw a student with a greater-than-even likelihood of not passing, which made your admission too risky for their program.

The single most important factor in this decision was your academic standing in the first year of school. You placed in the very bottom decile, while students who were accepted typically sat around the middle of the pack. This alone strongly pushed the model toward predicting bar exam failure. The second most influential factor was your third-year decile. While you improved slightly to the second decile, that was still far below the average of roughly the sixth decile among accepted students. The model interpreted this as continued academic struggle, reinforcing the prediction of failure.

Your full-time enrollment status, by contrast, actually helped you. Graduating from a full-time program tends to be associated with better preparation and lower risk, so this factor nudged the prediction toward passing. However, it was not enough to outweigh the very weak performance indicated by your class ranks. Other factors, such as your LSAT score and undergraduate GPA, were less influential in this decision, though they also sat below the averages of typical admits.

To improve your chances going forward, focus on raising your academic standing in your final years of school. A strong upward trend would directly address the most important concerns. Also consider strengthening your application with a serious bar exam preparation plan, and if possible, retake the LSAT after additional study. Demonstrating that you can succeed academically is the clearest path to a different outcome.
